abstract: Abstract Mechanophores provide an in situ and remote tool for quantifying invisible stress in polymers by photonic signals, offering distinct advantages for stress distribution analysis of large-area surfaces and instrument-free stress observation. However, achieving an ideal mechanophore that integrates with sensitive, reversible, and molecular-level stress sensing is attractive yet challenging. Here, we report practical guidance for developing ideal mechanophores that promote the molecular probe’s exciton transition for room-temperature phosphorescence (RTP) under stress, through the “assisted lowest triplet (T1) state” of the adjacent polymer chain. Systematic analyses of numerous organic probes reveal that a small energy gap (ΔEM < 0.4 eV) between the probe’s lowest singlet (S1) and the polymer’s T1 states is an empirical guideline for stress-enhanced RTP. The probe-doped polymer system demonstrates not only a remarkable increase in RTP intensity of over 2000-fold upon 160 MPa but also a low stress threshold of ∼2 MPa, which is robust under 0–10 MPa cyclic pressure loading/unloading over 500 cycles. Such RTP mechanophores enable noninvasive, reversible, and molecular-level stress detection in polymers. Their doped polymers have shown potential applications in various fields for real-time sensing of stress and its uneven distribution through visual afterglow.
hook: A polymer additive glows over 2000 times brighter under stress, mapping force as afterglow.
summary: Chemists tuned phosphorescent probes so squeezing a doped polymer makes it glow, guided by a small energy gap between probe and polymer states. The glow works from about 2 MPa and survived 500 pressure cycles. The design rule is empirical, drawn from a set of probes in lab samples.
title: Molecular Mechanophores Based on Stress-Enhanced Exciton Transition between Phosphorescent Probes and Polymer Matrix
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society
